The Core Assaying ProcessGate-Entry & Lotting: When a farmer unloads their produce, the mandi staff generates a unique Electronic Lot ID.Scientific Sampling: Rather than inspecting the entire heap, licensed assayers extract a composite sample from different layers of the pile to ensure a fair representation.Lab Testing: The sample is tested inside the e-NAM Assaying Laboratory at the APMC yard. Traditional physical appraisals are increasingly being replaced by advanced Near-infrared (NIR) Spectrophotometer machines to test parameters like moisture and oil content in under a minute 2. Primary Grading ParametersDifferent commodities feature specific tradable parameters defined under national rules. For instance, a standard crop like Wheat is analyzed across strict boundaries: [1] (https://www.ccsniam.gov.in/img/Benefit-of-eNAM-process-to-Farmer-A-Study.pdf), [2] (https://wdra.gov.in/documents/d/wdra/wheat_enam)Moisture Content (% by weight): Dictates storage longevity. Range-1 (Premium) requires a maximum of 11.0% moisture, whereas anything above 14.0% falls into lower tiers.Foreign Matter (% by weight): Tracks non-grain materials like stones, chaff, or dust. Lower percentages command a higher grade.Admixture & Other Edible Grains: The presence of alternative grain variants mixed into the primary batch.Immature & Shriveled Grains: Defective or underdeveloped grains that reduce total weight and crop yield quality 3. Price Discovery & Market ImpactTier Classification: Crops are labeled into Range-1, Range-2, or Range-3 depending on test outputs. High-quality, uniformly graded lots consistently secure 10% to 30% higher premium prices relative to ungraded heaps.Buyer Transparency: The final digital assaying certificate along with physical photographs of the lot is uploaded directly to the e-NAM bidding network. This allows remote traders, food processing industries, and corporate buyers to bid confidently without physically examining the lot

The Agricultural Produce Market Committee (APMC) Mandi rules govern how agricultural produce is traded, priced, and managed across standard wholesale market yards in India. Every state is divided into specific geographical market areas managed by an official Mandi Market Committee.Farmers must register ahead of time (submitting land, crop, and identity details) to bring and sell their produce inside the mandi gates.To curb tax evasion and regulate stock movements, farmers in multiple states must complete biometric verification, iris scans, and log vehicle registration numbers at the mandi gate before unloading.All bulk trading inside the market yards must be done strictly via open public auctions or electronic bidding to discover fair prices transparently.Buyers, wholesalers, commission agents (Arhtiyas), and weighmen must hold a valid state-issued license to trade inside the yard.Authorized weighmen must use standard government-verified weighing scales to weigh the crop.Traders are legally mandated to pay farmers on the same day of the transaction via direct bank transfer or authorized payment modes.Only statutory, government-notified fees (such as standard commission percentages, cleaning charges, and market taxes) can be deducted from the payout; unauthorized deductions are illegal.Under national e-NAM (electronic National Agriculture Market) rules, produce is sampled and undergoes physical quality assaying before its unique lot ID goes up for nationwide electronic bidding.Amendments to specific state Mandi Acts allow traders to buy directly from farmers' doorsteps or private cold storages via a single, unified state-wide trade license.Certain high-volume commodities like specific fruits and vegetables have been exempted from mandi fee rules in multiple states to encourage direct open-market sourcing.The local Mandi Market Committee acts as the official dispute resolution arbitrator to settle disagreements regarding weights, quality grades, or delayed payments between the buyer and the seller.
